title: Total beginner. Just built my own AI homelab and want to get into AI trading. Where do I start?
author: Least-Friendship4702
selftext:
Hey everyone, I'm brand new to this, so go easy on me 😅

I just finished building a dedicated AI box at home and I want to use it for automated trading, but I don't really know the right way to set it up.

My setup:

\- Ryzen 5 8500G, 16GB DDR5

\- AMD Instinct MI50 (16GB)

\- Running local Qwen models (Ollama / LM Studio)

\- Linux, on 24/7, remote access through Tailscale

\- Accounts on Robinhood and Coinbase

What I have so far: a basic Python bot running in paper mode (fake money). It's a simple trend strategy (EMA crossover + RSI with stop-losses), and my local LLM reviews each trade before it goes through. Backtests show the fast/hourly version just bleeds money to fees, and the slow daily version barely makes anything, so I know I'm missing a lot.

My questions:

1. What's the right role for a local LLM in trading? Should it make the trade decisions, filter trades, read news/sentiment, or something else?

2. Is Robinhood/Coinbase fine for bots, or should I switch to something like Alpaca or IBKR?

3. How long did you paper trade before going live, and how much did you start with?

4. Any good resources (books, YouTube, GitHub repos) for learning backtesting the right way and not fooling myself?

5. Biggest beginner mistakes you'd tell me to avoid?

I'm not expecting to get rich. I just want to learn this the right way and not blow up my account. Any advice is appreciated 🙏

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
I’d keep Qwen out of order approval initially. An LLM can produce different judgments from the same input, which makes it difficult to tell whether the EMA crossover + RSI rules work or whether prompt variation changed the result. A safer first role is summarizing news or explaining why a deterministic rule fired, with no ability to alter size, stops, or execution.

Since the hourly version already loses to fees, log the quoted spread, assumed fill, commissions, and next tradable price for every paper order. Promote only after a predeclared unseen period passes fixed drawdown and after-cost expectancy limits, not after an arbitrary number of profitable weeks.

comments.author: BetInformal6081
comments.body: if your backtests already lose money after fees that's useful information not failure try walk forward testing and compare your strategy against a simple buy and hold baseline before adding complexity..

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Nice setup. I'd use the local LLM for reading news or filtering ideas, and keep the actual rules, position size and stops in plain code so the model can't change them. Your backtest finding is useful, since fees kill fast strategies, so test with fees and slippage included and compare against simply holding. I haven't traded live with a bot myself, but I'd paper trade for a few months, then start with a small amount you can afford to lose. Cymetica lets you connect your own AI agent and starts it in paper mode, which is another place to practice.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
keep the Qwen models out of the buy and sell call at first. they're good at turning news into a score, but entries should be a plain rule you can backtest, or you can't tell luck from skill.

I built Quantradin with that split in mind, it grades a rule on past US stock and options prices, free, no real money. quantradin.com

will the MI50 be scoring news or picking entries?

comments.author: k1_r1
comments.body:
your backtest result is honestly the most useful thing in the post. hourly bleeding to fees and daily barely making anything usually means ema + rsi doesn't have much edge by itself, and having qwen review each trade won't add one. i'd keep the llm on news/sentiment and leave entries, sizing and stops in plain python like leroylabs said.

on 3, i'd want the paper run to include at least one ugly stretch (a month of chop or a real selloff) before any real money. alpaca is a lot easier than robinhood if you want to place orders from code.

if you want to test strategy ideas without building all the plumbing first, portfoliolab has free backtesting and paper accounts. i'm involved there so grain of salt

comments.author: Technical-Athlete-9
comments.body:
\#1 there are better approaches to most things in live trading decisions than LMs, but little as useful in research and analysis. The exception I could see is if you want to automate trading on news/announcements/filings. Even then I’d recommend other techniques because you’ll be competing on very small timeframes (too small to compete with free feeds) and that setup wouldn’t be fast enough. Maybe the LLM could periodically update your read on conditions and news so you don’t mistake a reaction to something beyond your view for an opportunity.

\#4 for a trader “Evidence Based Technical Analysis” by Aronson is probably the single best resource. There are good papers on backtesting properly as well - I asked an LLM to dig some up for me and found some useful ideas, but everything you need is in Aronson.

Follow Aronson to not fool yourself in research. Use LLMs to help Implement rules and to stay on course with rigor in your research. Use deterministic rules to trade.
